# What Zarr is {#sec-overview .unnumbered}

Zarr is a format for arrays with the model of HDF5
([](hdf5.qmd#sec-overview)): groups, arrays, which HDF5 calls datasets, and
attributes, with every array cut into chunks. It differs in where the data
lie. HDF5 is a file system in a file, with the chunks as blocks inside it and
an index of where each lies; Zarr uses the file system itself (@fig-store). A
group is stored as a directory, which holds arrays and other groups. An array
is stored as a directory as well: a file `zarr.json` in it describes the
array, and every chunk, a block of its values such as the map of one day, is a
file of its own. As in HDF5, an array holds values of one type with any
number of dimensions.
An attribute is a small named value on a group or an array, kept in its
`zarr.json`. In a cloud store, such as Amazon S3, the directories are prefixes
of names, such as `s3://bucket/ocean.zarr/`, and the files are objects.

![The results of the ocean model of the figure in *HDF5*, as a Zarr store, `ocean.zarr`. Every group and every array is a directory, with a file `zarr.json` that describes it and holds its attributes. Every chunk of an array, here the map of one day, is a file of its own. The arrays of the runs are shown for `run_01/` only.](figures/store.svg){#fig-store}

Zarr takes over from HDF5 where the one file is in the way. Because every chunk
is a file of its own, many processes can write one array at once, and a reader
can fetch single chunks over a network, from a cloud store; almost everything
that sets Zarr apart follows from that (@sec-storage). Where the one file is an
advantage, to send, archive, or publish data, HDF5 stays the simpler choice.
Working with Zarr comes down to writing and reading slices of arrays, mostly
through xarray (@sec-usage).

Zarr is at home in climate and earth observation data, and in microscopy, as
OME-Zarr. In Python, zarr-python reads and writes it, and xarray, with Dask,
works on it with named axes; in R, Rarr of Bioconductor reads and writes it,
and libraries in other languages, such as Julia, C++, and Java, too. Tables
belong in [](parquet.qmd) instead.

Checked against zarr-python 3.4, xarray 2026.9, Dask 2026.8, and Rarr 2.0.


# How Zarr stores arrays {#sec-storage}

The `zarr.json` of an array describes it completely: its shape, its type, the
shape of its chunks, its compression, its fill value, the names of its axes,
and its attributes. A chunk is named by its position in the grid of chunks,
such as `c/0/0/0` for the first day of `temperature` and `c/364/0/0` for the
last. Unlike HDF5, Zarr so needs no index of where the chunks lie: a reader
reads the `zarr.json` first, works out the names of the chunks that hold a
slice, and the file system or the cloud store finds them by name.


## Read only the chunks you need, over a network too {#sec-chunks}

As in HDF5, a slice reads and decompresses only the chunks it touches, and the
shape of the chunks decides which slices are fast
([](hdf5.qmd#sec-chunks)). Because every chunk is a file or an object of its
own, a reader fetches them one by one and in parallel, from a disk, a web
server, or a cloud store: the map of one day, from an array of terabytes in the
cloud, downloads one chunk. Every request over a network takes time, so chunks
of Zarr are best larger than those of HDF5, of about 1 to 100 MB.


## Many writers, no locks {#sec-writers}

Processes that write different chunks write different files, so many processes
may write one array at once, without locks, such as the jobs of a Slurm array,
each writing its days. Two processes that write into the same chunk, however,
overwrite each other: each reads the chunk, changes its part, and writes the
chunk back, and the part of the first is lost without an error. Neither Zarr
nor xarray prevents it. Let every process write whole chunks, by cutting the
work along the borders of the chunks.


## Missing chunks read as the fill value {#sec-fill}

Zarr does not write a chunk that holds only the fill value, and it reads a
chunk that does not exist as the fill value. A missing chunk is therefore
normal, not an error: a job that failed, a chunk lost in a copy, or a region
that nobody wrote reads as the fill value, 0 by default, without an error
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-loud)). The metadata are written when the
array is created, so the array has its full shape from the start. Give arrays
of floats the fill value NaN, as xarray does, so that what was never written
reads as missing ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-missing)).
`nchunks_initialized` counts the chunks that exist, which tells a complete
array from an incomplete one, as long as no chunk holds only the fill value.


## Many small files {#sec-files}

One file per chunk adds up: an array of a terabyte in chunks of a megabyte is a
million files. The file systems of clusters limit the number of files per user
and are slow with many small ones, and copying or deleting such a directory
takes long. Use larger chunks, or shards: Zarr 3 stores many chunks in one
file, a shard, and still reads them one by one. To move or archive an array,
zip its directory, without compression, because the chunks are compressed
already; zarr-python reads the zip file as it is (@sec-inspect).


## Two versions of the format {#sec-versions}

Zarr has two versions of its format, 2 and 3, with different files: version 2
describes an array in `.zarray` and `.zattrs`, and version 3 in `zarr.json`.
zarr-python 3 and xarray write version 3 by default, but some readers, in
other languages or older versions, read only version 2. Write version 2, with
`zarr_format=2`, for a reader that needs it. Shards and the names of the axes
in the metadata exist only in version 3, and not every reader of version 3
reads shards, such as Rarr in R (@sec-r).


# Working with Zarr {#sec-usage}

zarr-python reads and writes arrays as NumPy arrays, by position. xarray adds
names and coordinates, and Dask reads and computes in parallel, chunk by chunk.


## Write and read with zarr-python {#sec-zarr-python}

```python
import numpy as np
import zarr

ocean = zarr.open_group("ocean.zarr", mode="w")
temperature = ocean.create_array(
    "temperature", shape=(365, 720, 1440), chunks=(1, 720, 1440),
    dtype="float32", fill_value=np.nan,
    dimension_names=["time", "lat", "lon"],
)
temperature.attrs["units"] = "degC"
temperature[0] = first_day                  # writes one chunk

temperature = zarr.open_array("ocean.zarr/temperature", mode="r")
first_day = temperature[0]                  # reads one chunk
```

Indexing an array reads or writes only the chunks of the slice, as in h5py
([](hdf5.qmd#sec-h5py)). Mode `"w"` replaces whatever is at the path, `"a"`
opens it to change it. `shards=(30, 720, 1440)` in `create_array` stores thirty
chunks to a file (@sec-files). A URL in place of the path, such as
`s3://bucket/ocean.zarr`, reads from a cloud store, with the package s3fs
installed.


## Named axes with xarray and Dask {#sec-xarray}

```python
import xarray as xr

ocean = xr.open_zarr("ocean.zarr")          # lazy, in the chunks of the store
mean_june = ocean["temperature"].sel(time="2024-06").mean("time")
mean_june.to_zarr("mean_june.zarr")         # computes and writes
```

`open_zarr` reads only the metadata and the coordinates: every other array
becomes an array of Dask, in the chunks of the store, and a computation reads
the chunks it needs, in parallel, when its result is written or `compute` is
called. xarray stores the names of the axes and the coordinates, such as the
dates, in the store, and selects by them ([](hdf5.qmd#sec-netcdf)). `to_zarr`
with `append_dim="time"` appends along the time axis, and with `region` writes
one part of an existing array, such as the days of one job (@sec-writers).


## Read in R {#sec-r}

```r
library(Rarr)

zarr_overview("ocean.zarr/temperature")
first_day <- read_zarr_array("ocean.zarr/temperature",
                             index = list(1, NULL, NULL))
```

Rarr, of Bioconductor, reads and writes Zarr arrays of both versions, but not
shards. Unlike rhdf5 for HDF5 ([](hdf5.qmd#sec-axis-order)), it keeps the axes
in the order of the store, the same as in Python, so the first day is
`index = list(1, NULL, NULL)`.


## Look inside {#sec-inspect}

```python
print(zarr.open_group("ocean.zarr").tree())           # groups and arrays
print(zarr.open_array("ocean.zarr/temperature").info) # chunks, compression
```

The metadata are JSON files, which any editor or `cat` shows, such as
`ocean.zarr/temperature/zarr.json`. A zip file of a store, made inside its
directory with `zip -0 -r ../ocean.zarr.zip .`, opens read-only, with
`zarr.open_group(zarr.storage.ZipStore("ocean.zarr.zip"), mode="r")`.
